entities.name: Metropolitan Opera House
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Metropolitan Opera in New York City is the largest classical music organization in the United States and among the world's great opera institutions, founded in 1880 when a group of millionaires unable to obtain boxes at the Academy of Music built their own opera house. The Met's current home at Lincoln Center (opened 1966) accommodates 3,800 and serves as the primary venue for grand opera in the Americas.

The original Metropolitan Opera House on Broadway (1883-1967) was the site of American premieres of many major operas and home to legendary singers including Enrico Caruso, whose voice defined operatic stardom in the early 20th century. Caruso's 1903 Met debut began a 17-year career there that established the Met as the world's premier destination for great voices. The Met's radio broadcasts, beginning in 1931, made opera accessible to millions across North America — the Saturday afternoon Met broadcasts (the longest-running commercial classical music program in American history) continue to this day.

The Met at Lincoln Center under Peter Gelb's leadership (from 2006) introduced HD cinema broadcasts to 70+ countries, making Met performances accessible to millions who cannot attend in person. The Met's $300+ million annual budget, 800 full-time employees, and 230+ performances per season make it the world's largest opera organization. Financial crises in 2020 (COVID closure) and ongoing labor-management disputes about costs reflect the fundamental challenge of sustaining grand opera in the 21st century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Metropolitan Opera's Saturday broadcasts from 1931 created America's mass opera audience, and its HD cinema broadcasts from 2006 extended grand opera to millions globally — making it the most influential disseminator of classical operatic culture.
